slides.title: Why HDFS Exists
slides.headline: A single machine cannot store or process petabytes — HDFS makes a cluster look like one disk
points: 2003 problem: Google needed to index the entire web — no single server had enough disk
Solution: split files into chunks, spread across hundreds of cheap commodity machines
HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) is the open-source version of Google's GFS
One API hides all the complexity — you read and write as if it were a local file system
slides.callout: HDFS is optimised for large sequential reads (analytics), not random writes (OLTP). It is not a replacement for a database.

slides.title: HDFS Architecture
slides.headline: One NameNode knows where every block lives — many DataNodes actually store them
points: NameNode — the master: stores file→block→node metadata entirely in RAM
DataNode — the workers: store 128 MB blocks; send a heartbeat every 3 seconds
Client — talks to NameNode to get the block map, then reads/writes directly to DataNodes
Secondary NameNode — checkpoints NameNode metadata (NOT a hot standby)
slides.callout: If the NameNode goes down, the cluster is blind — HA mode runs an Active + Standby NameNode with ZooKeeper failover.
slides.arch:
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │         NameNode (Master)        │  ← Metadata in RAM
  │  /user/consultant/cc_fraud.csv   │
  │  Block A → DN1, DN2, DN3         │
  │  Block B → DN2, DN3, DN1         │
  └──────┬──────────┬────────────────┘
         │heartbeat │block report
    ┌────▼────┐ ┌───▼─────┐ ┌─────────┐
    │DataNode1│ │DataNode2│ │DataNode3│
    │Block A  │ │Block A  │ │Block A  │  ← 3× replicated
    │Block C  │ │Block B  │ │Block B  │
    └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘

slides.title: Block Storage & Replication
slides.headline: Every file is split into 128 MB blocks — each block lives on 3 different nodes
points: Block size 128 MB — a 500 MB file becomes 4 blocks spread across the cluster
Replication factor 3 — each block is copied to 3 DataNodes for fault tolerance
Rack awareness — HDFS places replicas on different server racks to survive rack failure
Losing one DataNode loses no data — the other two replicas take over immediately
slides.callout: Storage cost of replication: a 1 TB dataset consumes 3 TB on disk. This is intentional — disk is cheap, data loss is not.
slides.arch:
500 MB file → 4 blocks (128 MB each)

  Block A  ──► DN1 (rack 1), DN2 (rack 1), DN3 (rack 2)
  Block B  ──► DN2 (rack 1), DN3 (rack 2), DN4 (rack 2)
  Block C  ──► DN3 (rack 2), DN4 (rack 2), DN1 (rack 1)
  Block D  ──► DN4 (rack 2), DN1 (rack 1), DN2 (rack 1)

  DataNode failure → NameNode triggers re-replication in minutes

slides.title: HDFS vs Traditional Storage
slides.headline: HDFS wins at scale and cost — but it makes different trade-offs than a database or NAS
points: vs NAS/SAN — HDFS has no single storage appliance bottleneck; scales by adding nodes
vs RDBMS — HDFS stores any format (CSV, Parquet, JSON, images); no schema required at write time
vs S3/ADLS — HDFS is co-located with compute (data locality = Spark reads local blocks)
Write-once — files cannot be edited in place; analytics workloads (read heavy) love this
slides.callout: Schema-on-read: HDFS stores raw data. Hive and Spark interpret the schema when they query it. This means one file can be read by multiple tools with different schemas.
slides.arch:
Traditional (scale-up)        HDFS (scale-out)
  ┌────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │  Big Expensive SAN │        │  Node1   Node2   Node3   │
  │  2 TB, one vendor  │   vs   │  2 TB  + 2 TB  + 2 TB   │
  │  single point fail │        │  add more nodes any time │
  └────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────────┘

slides.title: ITC Use Case — cc_fraud Pipeline
slides.headline: 100k credit card transactions travel from PostgreSQL through HDFS to Hive and Spark
points: Source: PostgreSQL table cc_fraud_trans (13.42.152.118:5432, testdb)
Sqoop imports the table daily into HDFS at /user/consultant/cc_fraud/raw/
Hive creates an external table over that HDFS path — no data movement
PySpark reads the Hive table, applies 10 transformations, writes curated layer back to HDFS
slides.arch:
PostgreSQL (source)
       13.42.152.118:5432
            │
            │  Sqoop (MapReduce over JDBC)
            ▼
  HDFS  /user/consultant/cc_fraud/raw/
            │
            ├──► Hive external table  (bd_class_project.cc_fraud_trans)
            │
            └──► PySpark job  ──► HDFS  /user/consultant/cc_fraud/curated/
                                          │
                                          └──► Hive curated table
                                               (cc_fraud_trans_curated)

slides.title: MapReduce — The Original Big Data Engine
slides.headline: MapReduce moves computation to where the data lives — not data to where the computation is
points: Map phase — each DataNode processes its local blocks in parallel (data locality)
Shuffle & Sort — the framework groups all identical keys across all nodes
Reduce phase — one function aggregates each key's values into a final result
YARN ResourceManager schedules all Map and Reduce tasks across the cluster
slides.callout: Spark has replaced MapReduce for most workloads — it runs 10-100× faster by keeping data in memory instead of writing to HDFS between stages.

slides.title: HDFS in the CDH Ecosystem
slides.headline: HDFS is the foundation — every compute engine in the stack reads from and writes to it
points: Hive — SQL queries that treat HDFS directories as tables
Spark — reads HDFS directly as DataFrames; writes results back to HDFS
Impala — in-memory SQL over HDFS, faster than Hive for ad-hoc queries
Oozie — schedules Sqoop and Hive jobs that move data through HDFS

slides.title: Fault Tolerance in Practice
slides.headline: A DataNode can die mid-job and the cluster continues without interruption
points: Heartbeat timeout — if a DataNode misses 10 minutes of heartbeats, NameNode marks it dead
Automatic re-replication — NameNode copies under-replicated blocks to healthy nodes
Job recovery — YARN reschedules failed Map/Reduce tasks on other nodes automatically
Safe mode — NameNode enters safe mode on startup until enough block reports arrive
slides.callout: Safe mode blocks all writes. If a restart leaves the cluster in safe mode, run: hdfs dfsadmin -safemode leave
slides.arch:
Normal state (3 replicas)
  DN1[A,B]  DN2[A,C]  DN3[B,C]

  DN2 dies
       │
       ▼
  NameNode detects: Block A under-replicated (2 copies)
  NameNode detects: Block C under-replicated (1 copy)
       │
       ▼
  NameNode instructs DN1 → copy Block A to DN3
  NameNode instructs DN1 → copy Block C to DN3
       │
       ▼
  DN1[A,B]  DN3[A,B,C,C]  ← re-replicated within minutes

slides.title: Key HDFS Commands Reference
slides.headline: Eight commands cover 90% of day-to-day HDFS work on the cluster
points: hdfs dfs -ls / -mkdir / -rm -r  →  navigate and manage directories
hdfs dfs -put / -get / -getmerge  →  move data between local and HDFS
hdfs dfs -cat / -tail  →  inspect file contents without downloading
hdfs dfsadmin -report  →  cluster health: live nodes, capacity, usage
slides.callout: Practice these in the Linux Shell lab before the Sqoop session. Every tool (Sqoop, Hive, Spark) writes to HDFS — you must be able to verify the output.

slides.title: HDFS — Key Takeaways
slides.headline: HDFS turns a rack of cheap servers into a reliable, scalable storage system for big data
points: NameNode = brain (metadata in RAM) — DataNodes = storage (128 MB blocks on disk)
3× replication = fault tolerance; rack awareness = survives entire rack failure
Write-once, read-many — designed for batch analytics, not transactional updates
Foundation of CDH stack — Hive, Spark, Impala, and Oozie all read/write HDFS
In ITC pipeline: cc_fraud_trans lives in HDFS at /user/consultant/cc_fraud/raw/
slides.callout: Practical lab: create a directory, upload the cc_fraud CSV, run WordCount, verify with hdfs dfs -cat. See the Notes tab for step-by-step commands.
